execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you *can* do, not what you *should* do
. . . Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that are trusted, improve the quality of research, and provide a good user experience is the hard part.
. . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, or for which task.
. . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.
. . . Closed-weight cloud-based models show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc)
. . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources) ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent
. . . Reproducibility crisis in health research
. . . LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking. # Working with LLMs from R ## ellmer We'll be using the `ellmer` R package for interacting with LLMs.
. . . Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.
. . . Building on `ellmer`, we can add model-agnostic support with users choosing the model to use. ## Unstructured chat `ellmer` supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` :::

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_ollama() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id created_at size capabilities 1 MedGemma:4b 2026-10-14 3338942556 completion,vision 2 gemma3:4b 2026-10-14 3350272403 completion,vision 3 qwen2.5:0.5b 2026-10-14 397821319 completion,tools 4 gemma3:1b 2026-10-14 806067407 completion ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'dplyr' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': filter, lag ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:base': intersect, setdiff, setequal, union ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} library(PhenotypeR) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Registered S3 method overwritten by 'CodelistGenerator': method from print.code_search omopgenerics ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} system_prompt <- "You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) chat_medgemma ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ── system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat We can work with a simple, unstructured, chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension clinical presentation encompasses elevated blood pressure readings, commonly assessed via ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or office blood pressure measurements. Symptoms range from asymptomatic to those associated with target organ damage (e.g., headache, dizziness, visual disturbances, chest pain, shortness of breath, peripheral edema). Key clinical features also include hypertension-related conditions like stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease. Patient risk factors influencing hypertension include age, genetics, ethnicity, obesity, physical inactivity, sodium intake, excessive alcohol consumption, and stress. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension prevalence varies by age, with increasing incidence from middle age onward. Higher rates are observed in African Americans, Hispanics, and individuals with a family history of hypertension or those residing in specific geographic regions. Socioeconomic factors, including access to healthcare and healthy food options, also contribute to disparities. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Bad idea: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my OMOP CDM?") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` For OMOP CDM, consider using ICD-10 codes such as I10 (Essential (Primary) Hypertension), I11 (Secondary Hypertension), I15 (Hypertensive Heart Disease), I17 (Renovascular Hypertension), I25 (Hypertensive Kidney Disease), I22 (Hypertensive Cardiovascular Disease), I40-I45 (Specific Hypertension), and potentially others depending on the specific manifestation of the condition. Consider using UMLS concepts or SNOMED CT for more granularity. ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( typical_symptoms = type_string("summarise typical symptoms"), confirmatory_test = type_string("summarise what test result would confirm diagnosis"), disqualifying_diagnoses = type_string("summarise what alternative diagnoses need to be ruled out") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $typical_symptoms [1] "often asymptomatic" $confirmatory_test [1] "elevated blood pressure readings (ABPM or office)" $disqualifying_diagnoses [1] "diagnoses that should be considered to exclude hypertension" ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can force results to be integers/ numbers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("What is the average age at diagnosis?"), proportion_male = type_number("What proportion (between 0 and 1) of patients diagnosed with hypertension are male?") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 60 $proportion_male [1] 0.5513638 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat But remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 45 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 53 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = -10 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can set temperature to zero and add a seed to get closer to reproducibility. (This generally works better for local models than when working with cloud models.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = system_prompt, params = params(temperature = 0, seed = 42) ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 ``` ::: ::: # Integrating LLMs with PhenotypeR ## Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models - Available to all of the OHDSI community
. . . - Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)
. . . - Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).
. . . - But 6+ months behind "state-of-the-art". (Although allows us to learn from experience of others) ## Human-in-the-loop - Designed to support the human phenotyper, not automate them away.
. . . - All LLM-generated artefacts can be inspected, reviewed, and edited.
. . . - Main use of LLM is to provide additional context making it easier to double-check results ## Phenotyping tasks > "A problem well stated is a problem half solved." > > Charles F. Kettering (1876 – 1958)
. . . Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Started with lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions . . . - Reviewing codes included that led to cohort inclusion . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results . . . Higher-risk tasks currently out-of-scope: - Searching for codes. . . . - Creating cohort logic. . . . - End-to-end phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$metadata $hypertension$metadata$phenotype_name [1] "hypertension" $hypertension$metadata$version [1] "1.0" $hypertension$metadata$created_by [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$metadata$created_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_by [1] "N/A" $hypertension$metadata$last_edited_date [1] "2026-10-20" $hypertension$metadata$source_of_information [1] "MedGemma:4b" $hypertension$clinical_profile $hypertension$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is a prolonged elevation of blood pressure in the arteries. Other terms used to describe hypertension include high blood pressure, and elevated blood pressure." $hypertension$clinical_profile$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "Hypertension is often asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur, they may include severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleeds, or visual disturbances. These symptoms are often associated with severely elevated blood pressure, such as hypertensive crisis." $hypertension$clinical_profile$assessment_diagnosis [1] "Hypertension is typically diagnosed through repeated measurements of blood pressure, with a reading of 140/90 mmHg or higher considered diagnostic. Blood pressure measurements should be taken in both arms and at rest, and during separate visits. Other tests may include a physical examination, electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests (such as a complete blood count, kidney and liver function tests, and lipid profile), and an ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) study. In some cases, echocardiography, electrocardiogram, renal function test and/or blood tests may be performed." $hypertension$clinical_profile$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial treatment for hypertension typically includes lifestyle modifications, such as adopting a healthy diet, regular physical activity, weight loss (if overweight or obese), and reducing sodium and alcohol intake. If lifestyle modifications are insufficient to control blood pressure, medications are typically prescribed. First-line medications include angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), diuretics, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers. The choice of medication depends on the individual patient's characteristics and the severity of their hypertension." $hypertension$clinical_profile$complications_prognosis [1] "Untreated hypertension can lead to serious complications, including heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, and peripheral artery disease. Complications may arise in the short, medium, and long term. Short-term complications include hypertensive crisis with end-organ damage. Medium-term complications include heart failure, kidney failure, or stroke. Long-term complications include cardiovascular death, kidney disease, or stroke. The prognosis for hypertension varies depending on the severity of the condition and the presence of other medical conditions. However, with appropriate treatment and lifestyle modifications, the risk of complications can be significantly reduced." $hypertension$clinical_profile$disqualifiers [1] "Conditions that may require the medical professional to consider different diagnosis includes essential hypertension and hypertensive crisis due to other causes. Other conditions that could be considered include secondary hypertension due to specific medical conditions or drug induced hypertension, such as drug use. The temporal relationship between these conditions is important to consider in the diagnostic process. For example, if a patient presents with high blood pressure and a new onset of headache, it is important to consider whether the headache is caused by hypertension or by another condition, such as a brain tumour or meningitis. In cases where more than one diagnosis is considered simultaneously, clinicians also need to consider how these conditions may be related." $hypertension$clinical_profile$epidemiology [1] "Prevalence of hypertension increases with age. It is more common in men than in women before menopause and in women after menopause. Risk factors include family history of hypertension, obesity, physical inactivity, diet high in sodium, and excessive alcohol consumption. Other risk factors include diabetes, kidney disease, sleep apnoea, and certain other medical conditions. Common comorbidities include heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, and peripheral artery disease." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Primary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension, essential hypertension, chronic hypertension" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Secondary hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure that is caused by an underlying medical condition. It is also known as secondary hypertension or hypertensive cardiovascular disease." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cds$`Resistant hypertension`$clinical_profile$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is defined clinically as blood pressure that is consistently above target despite the use of three or more antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses. Other terms used include difficult-to-control hypertension, uncontrolled hypertension, and refractory hypertension. These terms are largely interchangeable." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(omock) library(CohortConstructor) library(PhenotypeR) library(gt) cdm <- mockCdmFromDataset(datasetName = "synpuf-1k_5.4", source = "duckdb") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ℹ Reading synpuf-1k_5.4 tables. ℹ Adding drug_strength table. ℹ Creating local object. ℹ Inserting into duckdb. duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: ℹ /Users/orms0426/.duckdb This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cdm$hypertension <- conceptCohort(cdm, list(hypertension = c(320128, 312648, 201826, 313217)), name = "hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: ! `codelist` cast to integers. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ℹ Subsetting table condition_occurrence using 4 concepts with domain: condition. ℹ Combining tables. ℹ Creating cohort attributes. ℹ Applying cohort requirements. ℹ Merging overlapping records. ✔ Cohort hypertension created. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} code_diag <- codelistDiagnostics(cdm$hypertension) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting counts of hypertension codes for cohort hypertension ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The CDM reference containing the cohort must also contain achilles tables. Tool calling ## Tool calling We can incorporate tool calling. But note we can't use them directly with structured chat. Here is a summary of the NICE approach to diagnosing hypertension: --- ### 1. Initial Clinic Blood Pressure Measurement * **Preparation:** Ensure the patient is seated, relaxed, and in a quiet environment. Palpate the radial or brachial pulse before measuring (if the pulse is irregular, measure blood pressure manually, as automated devices may be inaccurate). * **Both Arms:** At the first assessment, measure blood pressure in both arms. If the difference in readings between arms is more than **15 mmHg**, repeat the measurements. If the difference remains more than 15 mmHg on the second measurement, use the arm with the **higher** reading for all subsequent measurements. * **Multiple Readings:** If the first clinic blood pressure reading is **140/90 mmHg or higher**, take a second measurement during the consultation. If the second measurement is substantially different from the first, take a third measurement. * **Recording:** Record the **lower** of the last two measurements as the clinic blood pressure. --- ### 2. Confirming the Diagnosis (ABPM or HBPM) Do not diagnose hypertension based on a single clinic visit unless it is a hypertensive emergency. * **If Clinic BP is between 140/90 mmHg and 180/120 mmHg:** * **Gold Standard – ABPM (Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring):** Offer ABPM to confirm the diagnosis. Ensure at least 2 measurements per hour are taken during the person’s usual waking hours (e.g., 08:00 to 22:00). Use the average value of at least **14 measurements** taken during waking hours to confirm the diagnosis. * **Alternative – HBPM (Home Blood Pressure Monitoring):** If the person is unable to tolerate ABPM, offer HBPM. The patient should take two consecutive measurements (at least 1 minute apart) while seated, twice daily (ideally morning and evening) for at least **4 days** (ideally 7 days). Discard the measurements taken on the first day and use the average value of all the remaining measurements to confirm the diagnosis. * **If Clinic BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher (Severe Hypertension):** * **Refer for same-day specialist review** if there are signs of: * Retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema (accelerated/malignant hypertension). * Life-threatening symptoms (e.g., new-onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury). * Suspected phaeochromocytoma (e.g., labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor, diaphoresis). * **If no same-day referral is indicated:** Carry out investigations for target organ damage as soon as possible: * If target organ damage is identified, consider starting antihypertensive drug treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM/HBPM results. * If no target organ damage is identified, confirm diagnosis using ABPM/HBPM (or repeat clinic BP within 7 days). --- ### 3. Diagnostic Thresholds (Staging) Hypertension is diagnosed and staged using **both** clinic and ABPM/HBPM averages: | Stage | Clinic Blood Pressure | **AND** ABPM / HBPM Average | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Stage 1 Hypertension** | 140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg | **135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg** | | **Stage 2 Hypertension** | 160/100 mmHg to 179/119 mmHg | **150/95 mmHg or higher** | | **Stage 3 (Severe) Hypertension** | **Systolic ≥ 180 mmHg** OR **Diastolic ≥ 120 mmHg** | *(Confirmed via clinical assessment/ABPM as above)* | *(Note: If Clinic BP is ≥ 140/90 mmHg, but the ABPM/HBPM average is < 135/85 mmHg, this is considered **White-Coat Hypertension**).* --- ### 4. Concurrent Assessments (While Waiting for Confirmation) While awaiting ABPM or HBPM confirmation, NICE recommends completing two vital assessments for all patients with suspected hypertension: 1. **Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:** Use a formal risk assessment tool (such as **QRISK3**) to estimate the patient's 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease. 2. **Investigations for Target Organ Damage:** * **Urine:** Test for haematuria using a reagent strip, and send a urine sample to test for the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) to check for proteinuria. * **Bloods:** Measure electrolytes, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and HbA1c. * **Eyes:** Examine the fundi for the presence of hypertensive retinopathy. * **Heart:** Arrange a 12-lead electrocardiograph (ECG) to check for left ventricular hypertrophy or other cardiac abnormalities. ``` ::: ::: ## Grounding with `ragnar` & `embed_google_gemini()` Instead of pasting all the NICE guideline into the prompt, `ragnar` chunks the document and uses `embed_google_gemini()` to index each chunk as a semantic vector in DuckDB: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ragnar) library(pdftools) chunks <- pdf_text(nice_url) |> paste(collapse = "\n") |> MarkdownDocument(origin = nice_url) |> markdown_chunk() store <- ragnar_store_create( location = ":memory:", embed = embed_google_gemini() ) ragnar_store_insert(store, chunks) ragnar_store_build_index(store) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_nice_rag <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt("You are an expert clinical phenotyper. Answer strictly using retrieved NICE NG136 excerpts.") ragnar_register_tool_retrieve( chat = chat_nice_rag, store = store, store_description = "NICE NG136 hypertension guideline chunks" ) chat_nice_rag$chat( "According to NICE NG136, what blood pressure thresholds define Stage 1 vs Stage 2 hypertension?" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ◯ [tool call] search_store_001(text = c("What are the blood pressure thresholds that define Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension?", ...) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ● #> [ ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> { ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "origin": "https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213", ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "doc_id": 1, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> "chunk_id": 16, ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> … ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` According to the **NICE NG136** guideline (*Terms used in this guideline*), the blood pressure thresholds that define Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension are: ### **Stage 1 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** Ranging from **140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg** * **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** Ranging from **135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg** --- ### **Stage 2 Hypertension** * **Clinic blood pressure:** **160/100 mmHg or higher**, but **less than 180/120 mmHg** * **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** **150/95 mmHg or higher** *(Note: A clinic systolic blood pressure of 180 mmHg or higher or a clinic diastolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg or higher defines **Stage 3 or severe hypertension**.)* ``` ::: :::
